item.content:encoded:
The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday.
It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so I get it. It happens. We're often prisoners of the moment and emotion is a real thing.
I do want to push back on a specific idea, though, as floated by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic:
Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything.
Now, be sure that this isn't to attack the writer there, as I have the utmost respect for him and he even said he doesn't love the idea. I can see a lot of people running with this, though, and I'll offer up my opinion that this just isn't a feasible idea for the Phillies.
First off, Harper has a no-trade clause and it's been pretty clear over the last several years that he's now Philly through-and-through and doesn't want to go anywhere. Schwarber also has a no-trade clause with his 10-and-5 rights and now has a family with two young children.
Let's say either or both would accept a trade. Would it help the Phillies other than salary relief?
Schwarber is a 34-year-old designated hitter heading into 2027 with four years and $132 million left on his deal. How many teams would give the Phillies anything of value while also taking on a large portion of the salary? The answer is not that many and it might be zero.
Harper needs to permanently go back to first base and he'll also be 34 years old next season. He has five years and roughly $125 million left on his deal. Again, how many teams would give good value back to the Phillies and salary relief? The number is higher than with Schwarber, but not by much.
This isn't to say neither player is good. Both are very productive offensively. In fact, they were the Phillies' only two good hitters this season. Harper had a 131 OPS+ and Schwarber was at 128 with 100 being the average player at getting on base and hitting for power. No other qualified players on the Phillies were in the vicinity of Harper or Schwarber. Only Bryson Stott at 98 even approached league average. Brandon Marsh finished at 90, Alec Bohm 87 and Trea Turner 81. Yuck.
Schwarber and Harper are much more valuable to the Phillies than they would be to any other team, given the circumstances. And, unless the Phillies are going full-on rebuild, they might as well play out the contracts and try to win with them.
If you look at how things are set up for next season with the pitching staff, a rebuild doesn't make sense.
- Jesús Luzardo made a turn toward ace this season. He's under team control through at least 2031.
- Cristopher Sánchez will likely finish in the top three of Cy Young voting. He's under team control through at least 2032.
- Zack Wheeler showed flashes of being really good while returning from an incredibly tough surgical procedure. He's signed for one more season. He could well return to ace form.
- Aaron Nola doesn't have a tradeable deal, but hey, he had a 10-start stretch with a 2.10 ERA late in the season.
- There were still inconsistencies, but Andrew Painter, at age 23, made big strides during the season and perhaps turned a corner with in Game 2 vs. the Braves. Next year could well be a breakout.
That's a five-man rotation and maybe one of the very best in the majors.
Jhoan Duran is a top-three closer, too.
The starting point here is a great rotation and closer combination, along with Harper and Schwarber being excellent hitters. That's a better nucleus than most teams have. Ownership is committed to doing what it takes to land a winner for the city of Philadelphia and Dave Dombrowski is a front office executive who has proven he's good at making good teams into champions.
Keep taking as many shots at the postseason as possible in hopes that one of these years, the hot streak lines up properly for a championship. We've seen a well-timed hot streak pay off in recent years for teams like the Nationals, Braves and Rangers -- and maybe it'll be the Padres this year? -- so we know it can happen. Hell, the 2022 Phillies were right there.
The team defense needs to improve and there should be some tinkering with the position players, but the foundation here is far too strong to bail on Schwarber and/or Harper, especially when it wouldn't improve the big-league roster in the near-term.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Diamondbacks takeaways. What to do with Ketel Marte, offseason upgrades
item.dc:creator: Nick Piecoro; Arizona Republic
item.description: The Diamondbacks' end-of-year press conferences on Thursday, Oct. 1, largely were dominated by talk of manager Torey Lovullo's return for another year. Coming off another playoff miss, it seemed possible Lovullo might be out. Instead, he received a two-year deal. Here is a look at a few other topics that were explored during his 20-plus minute session with reporters. Will Ketel Marte be back f
item.content:encoded:
The Diamondbacks' end-of-year press conferences on Thursday, Oct. 1, largely were dominated by talk of manager Torey Lovullo's return for another year. Coming off another playoff miss, it seemed possible Lovullo might be out. Instead, he received a two-year deal.
But there were a few more nuggets that came from general manager Mike Hazen's portion of the afternoon. Here is a look at a few other topics that were explored during his 20-plus minute session with reporters.
Will Ketel Marte be back for another season?
Hazen sidestepped any questions about Marte's future, saying he had yet to take a look at roster construction for next season. But he did seem to acknowledge the argument for moving on from him after another season in which Marte created drama for an unexcused absence.
"I think you win with star players in this game," Hazen said. "But I am also — I've said this — I'm not blind to what the clubhouse dynamic is and what the interaction between all the players and the coaches and how that comes into winning and losing games."
Moreover, in the days surrounding Marte's return from the restricted and injured lists in late August/early September, players seemed to intimate that they expected Marte to be moved over the winter. Multiple players made comments about getting through the year and "dealing with the situation" after the season.
Where does the blame fall for 2026?
As is often the case, Hazen largely took responsibility for the team falling two games short of a playoff appearance with an 86-76 record. He made multiple references to not doing enough in the offseason to add to the first base and designated hitter positions and to the moves he was unable to make at the trade deadline, including upgrading those positions and adding a starting pitcher.
"Clearly didn't do enough," he said. "Left the team naked in places that it didn't need to be left naked, and we fell short by a game or two. I could go back and look at a million different ways where one or two things lead to one or two more wins, but that's one of them, too."
He also noted the fact that his team has had some tough luck in recent playoff misses. In 2024, they won 89 games but missed out via tiebreakers against the New York Mets and Atlanta Braves. And then this year they won more than three of the six teams that reached the postseason in the American League.
"It's hard for me to criticize 89 wins as, like, a failed season, even though you don't make the playoffs," he said. "It's hard for me to have more wins than half the American League playoff teams and just say that we were a failure when we all play the same schedule. But there's no excuse. We didn't make it."
What roster moves will they look to make this offseason?
The first area Hazen noted was a fairly obvious one: the need to improve against right-handed pitching, namely in the aforementioned first base/DH roles. Both were obvious areas of weakness this season.
Against right-handed pitching, the Diamondbacks hit .235/.309/.388 for a .697 OPS that ranked 26th in the majors. They had the lowest OPS at first base (.636) and the third-lowest at DH (.630) in the majors.
"The offseason priorities, from an add standpoint, are certainly going to be somewhere being a little more left-handed," Hazen said. "We struggled versus right-handed pitching this year. So that's a clear and obvious one."
Hazen also made a reference to wanting to "continue to improve our defense," though he acknowledged that might be a more "subtle" upgrade, perhaps suggesting he wants stronger bench/depth options than what the Diamondbacks had this year.
This article originally appeared on Arizona Republic: Diamondbacks takeaways. What to do with Ketel Marte, offseason upgrades

item.content:encoded:
Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong makes honest admission about struggles in NL Wild Card against Padres originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
It was a disappointing Wild Card series for the Chicago Cubs against the San Diego Padres, to say the least, and they were eventually swept.
The Cubs were unable to do anything on either side of the baseball for the better part of this series, with the offense being the biggest issue.
Chicago entered this Wild Card series with a chance to make some noise in the postseason, but the offense went absolutely quiet.
Expected National League MVP Award winner Pete Crow-Armstrong struggled just as much as anybody on the Cubs roster. Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-7 with four strikeouts, walking just once in the series, putting together a stolen base after that one walk.
Speaking to reporters after the game, the Cubs' 24-year-old superstar understands that he needed to be better, and while anybody can look at any numbers they want, it was obvious that he didn't contribute.
"We were challenged this year," Crow-Armstrong said, per The Athletic. "This team showed a lot of heart and a lot of fight through all the challenges. But I would say, to start: I show up. I show up when it matters in these games. That would help us immediately. But that's all I got right now."
"You can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute," Crow-Armstrong said.
Crow-Armstrong has never been the type of guy to beat around the bush and say he didn't do what was needed on both sides of the ball.
Unfortunately for the young man, this was a very disappointing series, one that he's going to have to live with throughout the remainder of the offseason. He had an incredible regular season, finishing the campaign with 45 home runs and a .943 OPS.
That wasn't even close to what he was able to do in the postseason.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs Won't Get Into ‘Bidding War’ For Seiya Suzuki
item.dc:creator: Joey Pollizze
item.description: It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling. The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world. It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter. However, the biggest question mark this offsea
item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

item.title: [Diario AS] Dodgers NLDS roster: Who will make the 26-man playoff roster against the Braves?
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Serrano; Jennifer Bubel
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles. Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeat
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Players Right About Questionable Decisions Against Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jon Conahan
item.description: The New York Yankees came away with an easy two-game sweep of the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round of the American League playoffs. The Yankees did exactly what they had to do on both sides of the baseball, completely dominating Boston when it came to the pitching side of things. Offensively speaking, the Yankees were just as great, scoring a combined 18 runs, putting up nine in each contest. The Yankees were able to do a lot of good in Wednesday night's win, but a lot of that was questione
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees came away with an easy two-game sweep of the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round of the American League playoffs.
The Yankees did exactly what they had to do on both sides of the baseball, completely dominating Boston when it came to the pitching side of things.
Offensively speaking, the Yankees were just as great, scoring a combined 18 runs, putting up nine in each contest. The Yankees were able to do a lot of good in Wednesday night's win, but a lot of that was questioned afterward by some of the players on the Red Sox. Some players clearly didn't feel like Sonny Gray should have been pulled, including Gray, who only threw 4.2 innings, allowing six hits and two earned runs.
Gray didn't walk any and struck out five. After coming out of the game, the Yankees offense was able to get going, putting together great at-bats against Erik Miller, Garrett Crochet, and Garrett Whitlock. As a whole, the three only pitched 1.2 innings, allowing eight hits and seven runs.
Willson Contreras and Gray had a lot to say about why they believed that shouldn't have been the case after the game.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do," Contreras said. "Because this is baseball, and the data is here to help us, but at the end of the day we're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time; I think that's a fact," said Gray, per The Athletic.
"Yeah, I mean, I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted. But what can you do, you know?"
As a competitor, it's not crazy to think Gray is right in a scenario like this.
It didn't feel like he had to be taken out in that scenario, but a lot of skippers and other decision-makers around Major League Baseball take guys out in moments like that when they're going through a lineup for the third time. It's one of those things that can either come back to haunt a team or be the right decision.
I'm personally not the biggest fan of not allowing Gray to stay on the mound, but that's just my opinion. It obviously worked out for the Yankees, but this was another time that showed that maybe a team should have trusted its gut instead of listening to an iPad.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Jacob Misiorowski vs. Padres: How Brewers Have Early NLDS Advantage
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy
item.description: After a few long days of waiting, we're finally just one day away from the Milwaukee Brewers kicking off their 2026 playoff run. Milwaukee will take the field on Saturday night against the San Diego Padres at American Family Field in Game 1 of the National League Division Series. It's been a long road to get here, but the playoffs have arrived and unsurprisingly, the first pitch of the postseason for Milwaukee will be from Jacob Misiorowski. The righty flamethrower was the best pitcher in baseba
item.content:encoded:
After a few long days of waiting, we're finally just one day away from the Milwaukee Brewers kicking off their 2026 playoff run.
Milwaukee will take the field on Saturday night against the San Diego Padres at American Family Field in Game 1 of the National League Division Series. It's been a long road to get here, but the playoffs have arrived and unsurprisingly, the first pitch of the postseason for Milwaukee will be from Jacob Misiorowski.
The righty flamethrower was the best pitcher in baseball throughout the 2026 season and he will have a chance to give Milwaukee an early lead in the series. The Padres aren't an easy matchup, to say the least. Fortunately, Misiorowski has already had some success against San Diego this season.
Misiorowski made a start against the Padres back on May 13. That day, the big righty tossed seven shutout innings and allowed just four base hits while striking out 10 batters. While that stat line is a bit absurd, it's pretty much in line with what he did all season to this point.
Jacob Misiorowski Give Milwaukee An Advantage
Misiorowski was the best pitcher in the league. There's no denying that fact. He finished the regular season with a league-leading 1.80 ERA to go along with 252 strikeouts in 174 2/3 innings pitched. The most earned runs he allowed in a game was five on Sep. 2. That was the only game in which he allowed more than three runs in a game all season. Simply put, he gave Milwaukee a chance to win every single time he touched the mound.
So, when it comes to Game 1, that's the guy you want to roll with. He was the best pitcher in baseball all season in general, plus he had individual success against the Padres. What else could you ask for?
Last season, the big flamethrower made three postseason appearances and had a 1.50 ERA in 12 innings of work. That was after struggling down the stretch and having his role shifted a bit with the organization. In the offseason, he went back to the lab and made a leap ahead of the 2026 season. If he pitches as he has all season to this point, Milwaukee should be able to come out on top in the first game of the five-game series. That's critical. Whoever wins Game 1 has a significant advantage the rest of the way in the series.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. item.description: The MLB Wild Card round, first round of the WNBA Playoffs and start to the NHL season went head-to-head on Tuesday, and baseball came away a big winner with the best game audience to start the first round in two decades. Yankees-Red Sox Game 1 in primetime on NBC drew 7.3 million viewers, which is the best Game 1 for any Wild Card or LDS game since Tigers-Yankees drew 8.4 million in the ALDS on Fox in 2006. The audience was up 12% from ESPN’s 6.5 million viewers for Game 1 of the same matchup in
item.content:encoded:
The MLB Wild Card round, first round of the WNBA Playoffs and start to the NHL season went head-to-head on Tuesday, and baseball came away a big winner with the best game audience to start the first round in two decades.
Yankees-Red Sox Game 1 in primetime on NBC drew 7.3 million viewers, which is the best Game 1 for any Wild Card or LDS game since Tigers-Yankees drew 8.4 million in the ALDS on Fox in 2006. The audience was up 12% from ESPN’s 6.5 million viewers for Game 1 of the same matchup in last year’s Wild Card round. Earlier in the day in the 2pm ET window, Braves-Phillies drew 3.9 million viewers on NBC, marking the best afternoon Game 1 since the current Wild Card format started in 2020. Figures were not yet available for the Peacock-exclusive games, which were much lower than the broadcast TV counterparts.
Up against MLB Wild Card games, Prime Video saw its best WNBA game audience yet, averaging 1.42 million viewers for Aces-Fever Game 2. That’s also up from 1.28 million for the Fever’s Game 2 against the Dream on ESPN last year in a similar window. Later on Tuesday night, USA Network and CNBC averaged a combined 1.06 million for Liberty-Lynx Game 2, up from 949,000 viewers for the comparable Aces-Storm Game 2 on ESPN last year.
The NHL opened its 2026-27 regular season with 859,000 viewers for Panthers-Hurricanes in the 5pm ET window on ESPN, up 16% from Blackhawks-Panthers in the same slot last year. In primetime, Rangers-Bruins drew 878,000 viewers on ESPN, down 19% from 1.09 million for Rangers-Penguins in the same slot in 2025. Rangers-Bruins had to deal with viewers in the markets likely watching the Yankees-Red Sox game.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Phillies 2B Luis Arraez's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
Any club pursuing three-time batting champion Luis Arraez will likely need a plan to play him regularly at second base.
In a 2026 season split between the San Francisco Giants and Philadelphia Phillies, Arraez returned to his natural position of second base. In terms of outs above average, he had the best season of his career, with San Francisco infield coach Ron Washington credited with helping his defensive growth.
Arraez should do better this offseason than the one-year, $12 million deal he settled for last offseason. He was unavailable for the Phillies' Wild Card Series loss to Atlanta because of a sprained left ankle, though the injury is not expected to affect his availability for 2027.
Let's take a look at the best potential landing spots for the four-time All-Star.
5. Texas Rangers
1 of 5
Whether the Rangers are in on Arraez will depend on whether managing partner Ray Davis authorizes president of baseball operations Chris Young to add payroll in the offseason.
From a baseball perspective, the Rangers' second basemen posted an OPS south of .700 this season. Clearly, Arraez would give them more offensively than they got in 2026.
Top prospect Sebastian Walcott is a shortstop/third baseman who is expected to play a role for the team in 2027. But even with Corey Seager at shortstop and Josh Jung at third base, Walcott seems more likely to play outfield than second base. There aren't many 6'4" second basemen.
4. Philadelphia Phillies
2 of 5
Arraez didn't perform as well with the Phillies as he did with the Giants, but his track record suggests that over a larger sample size, he will hit for a higher average.
The Phillies dealt pitching prospects Ramon Marquez and Marty Gair to acquire Arraez and reliever Caleb Kilian, so they should at least consider a reunion in free agency.
That said, some of this will come down to how the Phillies want to set up their infield in 2027. Alec Bohm will likely depart in free agency, while Bryce Harper is expected to return to first base.
Will the Phillies move Trea Turner off of shortstop, and if so will that be to second base or left field? What about Bryson Stott, whom the team likes at second base but moved to third to accommodate Arraez? Also looming is top prospect Aidan Miller, who missed most of 2026 but is an exciting bat who can play shortstop or third base.
Many moving parts make it unclear whether the Phillies will commit to multiple seasons of Arraez at second base. Still, his presence behind Bryce Harper gave Philadelphia a contact-oriented option in the heart of its lineup and may have made it easier for Harper to remain selective at the plate.
3. Pittsburgh Pirates
3 of 5
Will the Pirates extend the qualifying offer to Brandon Lowe? It's always difficult to know how owner Bob Nutting will operate. Even if the QO goes to Lowe, one would think he'd decline it in search of a multi-year commitment.
If Lowe ends up not returning to Pittsburgh, the Buccos will have a hole at second base. One way to soften the negative reaction to not bringing Lowe back after an excellent contract year is to sign a replacement as accomplished as Arraez.
You could do worse than a middle-infield pairing of Arraez and Konnor Griffin, especially in terms of offensive production.
2. San Francisco Giants
4 of 5
It's rare but not unheard of for a player to get traded midseason and then return to the club that traded him in the offseason as a free agent. This might be one of the instances where it makes sense, though.
Arraez not only built a great relationship with the aforementioned Washington, but he also hit .324 in 105 games with the Giants. While home run hitters other than Barry Bonds don't love Oracle Park, Arraez's offensive profile fit the park well. In 49 games at Oracle Park in 2026, Arraez hit .361.
This may come down to whether the Giants are comfortable with Casey Schmitt playing elsewhere on the diamond so Arraez can resume as the team's second baseman. Offensively, Arraez remains a great fit for the Giants.
1. Detroit Tigers
5 of 5
The Tigers will have quite a bit of money coming off the books this offseason, including the $22.025 million that Gleyber Torres made after accepting the qualifying offer last winter.
Arraez spent the first four seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins, so a return to the AL Central could make sense. It's a bit surprising that Arraez has hit only .265 in 88 career plate appearances at Comerica Park, but the spacious outfield suits a contact hitter.
Additionally, with Torres coming off the books, the Tigers will have an opening at second base. Adding Arraez's bat-to-ball skills could help Detroit rebound from a disappointing 2026.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs’ Dansby Swanson Says Goodbye To 4-Time Gold Glove Teammate After Brutal Exit
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Chicago Cubs entered the 2026 postseason with legitimate expectations of making another deep October run. Instead, their season ended abruptly in San Diego, leaving the organization to confront a disappointing Wild Card exit and some difficult questions about what comes next. The Cubs were swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Series, falling 4-1 in Wednesday's decisive game at Petco Park. The loss ended a season in which Chicago returned to the playoffs for a second
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Cubs entered the 2026 postseason with legitimate expectations of making another deep October run. Instead, their season ended abruptly in San Diego, leaving the organization to confront a disappointing Wild Card exit and some difficult questions about what comes next.
The Cubs were swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Series, falling 4-1 in Wednesday's decisive game at Petco Park. The loss ended a season in which Chicago returned to the playoffs for a second consecutive year, but it also brought the future of several important veterans into sharper focus.
Among them is Ian Happ, the longest-tenured player on Chicago's active roster and a four-time Gold Glove winner in left field.
"Happ was drafted by the Cubs in the 2015 MLB Draft and has spent his entire professional career with the Cubs ever since," Alex Dvorak noted for NBC 5 Chicago. "But he is expected to become a free agent in 2027, leaving his future with the team uncertain."
After the loss, franchise shortstop Dansby Swanson offered an emotional assessment of what Happ has meant to the Cubs and to him personally.
Chicago Cubs Star Dansby Swanson Reflects On Ian Happ's Cubs Legacy After Exit
With Happ potentially ending his Cubs career with a brutal postseason sweep, Swanson was asked immediately after the game what his teammate has meant to him.
"That's a tough one," Swanson said, getting noticeably choked up in a clubhouse interview with Marquee Sports Network. "He's meant a lot to me. I think he truly embodies what it means to wear the jersey."
Happ debuted with the Cubs in 2017 and developed into an established veteran, earning an All-Star selection in 2022 and four consecutive Gold Glove Awards from 2022 through 2025.
That defensive consistency became one part of Happ's identity in Chicago, but his importance to the organization extends beyond his production. He has been through multiple versions of the Cubs and remained a fixture as the franchise rebuilt around a younger core.
Swanson, who joined Chicago before the 2023 season, clearly developed a particularly close relationship with Happ.
"He's probably my longest friend that I've had here, so yeah, that probably speaks enough for itself," Swanson added. "He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know so he's a big reason why I'm here and I'm very thankful for him."
Chicago Cubs Face Ian Happ Decision After Playoff Exit
Following the unceremonious playoff exit, Happ is now among the Cubs players whose futures could become a significant offseason storyline, meaning Wednesday's loss may have been the final game of his Chicago tenure.
That possibility helps explain the emotion surrounding Swanson's comments. Happ has become closely associated with the Cubs since entering the organization as a first-round pick, and his potential departure would remove one of the most familiar faces from a clubhouse that just experienced another disappointing postseason ending.
After a season that ended far earlier than Chicago hoped, Swanson's goodbye captured the significance of the franchise's longest-tenured players.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] The Red Sox lost, but is the Sox-Yankees rivalry inching back toward center stage?
item.dc:creator: Bryan Joiner
item.description: Forget the results, if you can. Losing two games in a row is a rounding error for a baseball team in every other month, but in October, it's definitive. Win and you're good. Lose and you're bad. In this telling, the Red Sox rapidly lost to the Yankees, ergo they're bad. item.content:encoded:
Forget the results, if you can. Losing two games in a row is a rounding error for a baseball team in every other month, but in October, it's definitive. Win and you're good. Lose and you're bad. In this telling, the Red Sox rapidly lost to the Yankees, ergo they're bad. I disagree, and this felt different to me, at least through the first six innings of both games, when things were still close enough. I felt like it was the beginning of the next great era of baseball's best rivalry.
Despite the result, I still think that.
Prior to this season — and maybe including it — I've felt that that the Red Sox/Yankees first-round playoff serieses haven't been all that consequential or compelling, because the teams are so obviously limited. I mean sure, playoff baseball widens the aperture of what's possible for good teams, but I thought neither team was likely to truly contend in 2021 or 2025, even with baseball's chaotic-by-design playoff system. This year is different. While the AL competition was so soft, like it was for last year's Patriots, both teams were plenty good enough to make the World Series, which is all you can ever ask.
The lack of Garrett Crochet and Aaron Judge left the series with a distinctly large cast of new main characters, personified by the starters, beloved Red Sox Nation blue-collar immigrant Payton Toll, despised Red Sox Nation white-collar emigrant elite Cam Schlittler and (sigh) Ben Rice. Central casting did its job for giving each fanbase its broadly-dreamt personification in a SP1, whether or not the personification has a representation in reality. we got what we wanted. The Yankees, with Rice and former MVP Cody Bellinger, got a little more, and their season continues.
But the broader question is: are we back? And not in a short-term sense? In the sense that the misery of the Yankees will return to the forefront of our minds on a daily basis? I hope so, because it's so much better that way. I think we are, after a needed cooling off period, and not just for the fans but for the owners and the league. Sometimes you need a moment alone. I live in suburban NY and they've hated the Astros since before COVID despite the multiple postseason matchups with the Sox, and I think older Red Sox and Yankees fans as a whole are happy for the interregnum on a broader horizon. Or maybe I'm just projecting, and it's certainly something I have enjoyed. I've had a break, and I'm ready to hate again.
That is, there's too much gold in these there hills to leave the rivalry comparatively dormant for so long. Not that you don't want to beat each other, every game, but the feeling of something far beyond that. This feeling, like a sourdough starter, needs time to regenerate; if it ends up taking 25-30 years, whih seems like an eternity in the moment, it's just sort of how it has gone on a longer time horizon. The last high point was 2003-2004, but before that it was Bucky Dent, in the fertile year of 1978. Before that, DiMaggio and Ted Williams in the pre- and post-war 1930s/40s era. Before that, 1918. So yeah. Every 25-30 years it happens. It doesn't have to be that way, but it just is.
On that schedule, I suspect or just wish we're due for a Retvrn to becoming the biggest story in baseball on a daily basis, and one that expands the reach of the game as effectively as Shohei Ohtani, who's done a decade's worth of heavy lifting. I am definitely wishcasting this toward existence, but I also think it's a real possibility for the next 5-to-10 years given how committed both organizations have been to similar projects in the last decade. Now they get to shut down the Dodgers by any means necessary this offseason and return to the top of the heap, even if they have to threaten the game's survival to do so. And you know what? They'll fuckin do it. If the Sox and Yankees aren't top of mind, it's gotta be a structural problem, right? Right?
True or not, both teams are so close to accomplishing a renovation that puts them back the center of baseball dialogue that we can almost taste it. If I'm right, the good news is that this year's loss, while a bummer, is still just an appetizer, and hopefully the last one. We're ready for the main courses. The divisional and LCS rounds beckon, and the identities of the post-teardown squads will further solidify. But the picture is coming in to focus: Schlittler will win the Cy Young; Tolle has won over everyone else. In this particularly illustrative case, the NY/Boston coding, as least as we'd like to conceive of it, is perfectly balanced, as all things should be. I hope this particular infinity war is ready to flare back up.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts. item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] La Batalla Por El Comodín Entre Los Yankees Y Los Red Sox Desata Una Guerra Política Y El Colapso Del Dueño De Barstool
item.dc:creator: Inna Zeyger
item.description: NUEVA YORK — Los Red Sox de Boston aguantaron dos noches en el Bronx. Las discusiones que dejaron atrás siguen en marcha. item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Los Red Sox de Boston aguantaron dos noches en el Bronx. Las discusiones que dejaron atrás siguen en marcha.
Los Yankees arrasaron en la Serie de Comodín de la Liga Americana en el Yankee Stadium, ganando 9-0 el martes y 9-2 el miércoles. Boston anotó dos carreras en 18 entradas.
Nueva York lo consiguió sin Aaron Judge. Max Fried y Cam Schlittler mantuvieron a los Red Sox a una sola carrera en 12 1/3 entradas. El jonrón de tres carreras de Cody Bellinger en una séptima entrada en la que se anotaron seis carreras acabó con cualquier duda en el segundo partido. Antes, Luis García Jr. rompió el empate a cero con un jonrón en la cuarta entrada ante Sonny Gray, y el as de Boston, Garrett Crochet, no consiguió eliminar a ninguno de los cuatro bateadores a los que se enfrentó.
La temporada de Boston había dado un giro radical. Los Red Sox despidieron al entrenador Alex Cora durante una racha que les dejó 14 partidos por debajo del 50 % a finales de junio. Respondieron con una racha de 15 victorias seguidas y un mes con un balance de 21-4 —récord de la franquicia— para alcanzar el puesto n.º 5.
Los Yankees han eliminado ahora a los Red Sox en dos postemporadas seguidas por primera vez. Nueva York lleva una ventaja de 4-3 en los siete enfrentamientos de postemporada, con victorias en 1999, 2003, 2025 y 2026.
Boston anotó cinco carreras en sus últimos cuatro partidos de playoffs contra los Yankees, todos disputados en el Bronx. El jonrón de Willson Contreras en el segundo partido puso fin a una sequía anotadora de los Red Sox en la postemporada de 26 2/3 entradas.
La mayoría de los años, la conversación pasaría directamente a la siguiente ronda. Esta vez, se fue por otros derroteros.
La temporada de Boston se había convertido en tema de conversación mucho más allá del Fenway Park. Una senadora estadounidense que luchaba por su supervivencia política había vinculado parte de su discurso a ella. Un magnate de los medios nacido en Massachusetts con millones de seguidores estaba dispuesto a defenderla.
El jueves por la mañana, ambos tuvieron que rendir cuentas ante un equipo de los Yankees que les había endosado un 18-2.
Un anuncio de campaña que apostaba por Boston
La senadora republicana Susan Collins, de Maine, aspira a un sexto mandato. Su campaña emitió un anuncio que utilizaba la rivalidad para enmarcar su contienda contra el líder de la minoría del Senado, Chuck Schumer, un demócrata de Nueva York y conocido seguidor de los Yankees.
El anuncio alterna entre imágenes del Fenway Park, un Schumer serio y Collins saludando a los votantes por todo Maine. La frase inicial parecía un informe de seguimiento sobre los Yankees.
«Los Red Sox saben cómo lidiar con los Yankees, y Susan Collins sabe cómo lidiar con Chuck Schumer, el súper fan de los Yankees», dice el narrador.
A continuación, el anuncio pasa del béisbol a la lealtad al estado natal. Presenta el equipo al que anima Schumer como prueba de cuáles son sus prioridades.
«Mientras Chuck Schumer anima a Nueva York, el equipo de Susan es Maine», dice el narrador.
Schumer es un blanco habitual de Collins porque los grupos demócratas vinculados a él han gastado mucho dinero en campaña contra ella. Una organización sin ánimo de lucro afiliada al Senate Majority PAC, vinculado a Schumer, invirtió 2 millones de dólares en anuncios contra Collins a principios de este año, según Axios.
Schumer responde a la guerra de anuncios contra los Yankees
Schumer tomó la palabra la mañana después de que se aseguraran el título. Cuando le preguntaron por la serie, se centró en la premisa del anuncio.
«No fueron los Yankees los que se quedaron en blanco las dos últimas noches», dijo Schumer.
El rival demócrata de Collins tampoco se libró de la serie. Troy Jackson, ex presidente del Senado de Maine y leñador del norte del estado, publicó su apoyo a Boston antes del primer partido.
«¡Vamos, Sox!», escribió Jackson en X.
La maniobra innecesaria de Portnoy
La segunda voz de Boston llegó tras el último out. El fundador de Barstool Sports, Dave Portnoy, natural de Massachusetts y seguidor de toda la vida de los Red Sox, vio cómo los Yankees celebraban en su vestuario y publicó su veredicto en X.
Portnoy se centró en la fiesta, no en el resultado. Las celebraciones con champán son habituales tras ganar una serie en la MLB, algo que una nota de la comunidad de X añadió más tarde a su publicación.
«Que los Yankees celebren con champán la victoria en la serie de comodines solo demuestra lo bajo que ha caído esa franquicia. Es muy vergonzoso», escribió Portnoy.
Un usuario sugirió que Portnoy publica una versión de la misma queja cada otoño.
«El tuit programado de cada año, jajaja. Seguro que programaste este el año pasado porque sabías que volvería a pasar», escribió un usuario de X.
En cifras: una primicia en la historia de octubre de esta rivalidad
Esta barrida le dio a Nueva York algo que nunca había conseguido contra Boston. Los Yankees han eliminado a los Red Sox en dos postemporadas seguidas por primera vez.
En siete enfrentamientos de postemporada, Nueva York lleva la delantera por 4-3, tras ganar en 1999, 2003, 2025 y 2026. Boston ganó en 2004, 2018 y en el partido de comodín de 2021.
En los últimos cuatro partidos de postemporada entre estos rivales, todos disputados en el Bronx, los Red Sox anotaron cinco carreras.
La temporada regular había apuntado en otra dirección. Boston encadenó una racha de 15 victorias seguidas y un mes con un balance de 21-4, récord de la franquicia, pero Nueva York se llevó la serie de la temporada por 7-6, coronada con una goleada de 16-1 en el último encuentro.
Los Rays son los siguientes, mientras la carrera por Maine sigue reñida
Los Yankees descansan dos días antes del primer partido de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana contra los Tampa Bay Rays, campeones de la División Este de la Liga Americana. El primer lanzamiento está previsto para las 18:30 h EDT del sábado en el Tropicana Field.
Tampa Bay tenía el mejor balance de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees acabaron con un balance de 6-7 contra los Rays durante la temporada regular. La disponibilidad de Judge sigue siendo la mayor incógnita en torno a la alineación y la plantilla del entrenador Aaron Boone.
Una encuesta de CNN/SSRS realizada a 880 votantes registrados, entre el 31 de agosto y el 6 de septiembre, mostró que Jackson iba por delante de Collins con un 48 % frente a un 45 %. El «Cook Political Report» califica la contienda como reñida.
Los dos candidatos sí que comparten una cosa: los dos son seguidores de los Red Sox.
La temporada de Boston ya ha terminado. La racha de los Yankees continúa este sábado en San Petersburgo, Florida. Los votantes de Maine acudirán a las urnas el 3 de noviembre.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [si.com] Unlikely Hero Ray Kerr Silences Phillies As Braves Advance to NLDS
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The Braves powered their way to an NLDS berth after taking out their division rivals. item.content:encoded:
The Braves powered their way to an NLDS berth after taking out their division rivals.
On Thursday night, Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 against the Phillies, 6–2, in front of a loud Truist Park crowd. The Braves tagged Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola for three runs in the bottom of the first inning and never looked back, leading wire-to-wire to eliminate their NL East peers.
Surprise starter Ray Kerr, a 32-year-old with 72 2/3 career MLB innings, pitched into the fourth inning unscathed to keep the Phillies at arm’s length. The Phillies never found much offense beyond contributions from stars Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, as the supporting cast beyond Alec Bohm failed to step up.
The victory sends Atlanta to Los Angeles for an NLDS matchup with the Dodgers starting on Saturday. For Philadelphia, a season that began with World Series ambitions was cut short in the wild-card round.
Here are our three takeaways from Game 3.
Braves Slug Their Way to NLDS
Atlanta relied heavily on the long ball in 2026, and with its season on the line that’s what it used to punch a ticket to the NLDS.
The Braves’ 204 regular season home runs ranked seventh in baseball, while their collective .409 slugging percentage was sixth. In Game 3, they flexed those muscles, blasting three home runs that accounted for each of their six runs.
Michael Harris II got things started in the bottom of the first, when he stepped to the plate with one out after back-to-back walks to Ronald Acuña Jr. and Matt Olson. He hammered a 2–0 sinker from Aaron Nola just over the right field wall to give Atlanta a 3–0 lead it wouldn’t relinquish.
Ozzie Albies got into the act three innings later when he launched a 96 mph four-seamer from Zack Wheeler 419 feet into the stands in right-center to increase the lead to 5–0.
Matt Olson added another in the seventh inning when he crushed a Jonathan Bowlan changeup to center to give Atlanta a 6–1 margin.
If the Braves are going to make a deep run in the playoffs, they’ll need to keep thumping baseballs out of the park. It’s the way they have played all year and it's how they were able to close out the Phillies.
The Ray Kerr Game
When the Braves announced their Game 3 starter, the collective response from the baseball world was: “Who?” We all know his name now.
Kerr had a remarkable path to signing with the Mariners as an undrafted free agent in 2017, at different points working at a movie theater and a 7-Eleven after dropping out of junior college. He bounced around the minors for several years and finally made his big league debut for the Padres at 27 years old in ’22, then recorded a 5.06 ERA in 29 games (32 innings) out of the bullpen over two seasons. He was then traded to Atlanta and recorded a 5.64 ERA in 10 games for Atlanta in 2024, but didn’t get back to the majors until Aug. 17 of this year. Once he did, he shined.
In nine appearances, he was 1–0 with a 1.47 ERA and a 0.60 WHIP. Still, he had three career starts entering Thursday night, and his team had never won any of them. The 32-year-old lefty made Atlanta manager Walt Weiss look like a genius Thursday night.
In his postseason debut, Kerr was locked in on the mound as he carved through a Phillies lineup loaded with All-Stars. He pitched 3 ⅓ shutout innings, allowing one hit, one walk and striking out two. Kerr left the game with a 3–0 lead. Atlanta’s rotation is banged up right now and they needed a big performance from whoever started Game 3. They got it from the last guy anyone expected.
Schwarber, Harper Get No Help
Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper brought the Phillies back from the dead in Game 2, hammering back-to-back home runs in the eighth inning to tie a game Philadelphia ultimately won in 10 innings. On Thursday night in Game 3, the duo combined to go 3-for-7 with a walk and a run scored. The rest of the lineup went 3-for-24 with two walks and a run. That wasn’t going to get it done.
As a team, the Phillies slashed .231/.270/.394 with 23 strikeouts over the three games, while Trea Turner went 1-for-11, Bryson Stott was 2-for-13 and J.T. Realmuto was 2-for-10. Alec Bohm was the only other hitter who showed up, going 4-for-12 with a home run. The offense that ranked 28th in wRC+ (92) during the regular season didn’t give enough support to its two main contributors, as the flaws that dogged the Phillies all year were predictably their undoing as they exited the postseason with a whimper.
If Philadelphia is going to keep its title window open, Schwarber and Harper need some help.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.title: [Audacy] Bryce Harper tras temprana eliminación de Filis: 'Vinimos a ganar y no lo hicimos'
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper no quiere pronunciar frases que comiencen con “si hubiera", “si pudiera” o ”debí haber". La conclusión para los Filis de Filadelfia es que volvieron a quedarse cortos en la postemporada. “Estamos aquí para hacer el trabajo. Estamos aquí para ganar juegos y no lo hicimos”, comentó Harper en un apagado clubhouse de los Filis la noche del jueves, tras su derrota por 6-2 ante los Bravos de Atlanta en el tercer y decisivo encuentro de su serie de comodines de la Liga Nacio
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper no quiere pronunciar frases que comiencen con “si hubiera", “si pudiera” o ”debí haber".
La conclusión para los Filis de Filadelfia es que volvieron a quedarse cortos en la postemporada.
“Estamos aquí para hacer el trabajo. Estamos aquí para ganar juegos y no lo hicimos”, comentó Harper en un apagado clubhouse de los Filis la noche del jueves, tras su derrota por 6-2 ante los Bravos de Atlanta en el tercer y decisivo encuentro de su serie de comodines de la Liga Nacional:
El toletero estelar no puso excusas por el bajón de septiembre que impidió a los Filis alinear su pitcheo contra Atlanta, porque necesitaron hasta el juego número 162 para asegurar un puesto en los playoffs.
Filadelfia forzó el tercer juego ante los Bravo con tres dramáticos jonrones solitarios en la recta final del segundo encuentro. Pero al final, los Filis cayeron en un hoyo temprano en el partido del jueves y quedaron eliminados de la postemporada por quinto año consecutivo, mientras persiguen su primer título de la Serie Mundial desde 2008.
Al mánager interino Don Mattingly le habría encantado poder organizar el pitcheo y que estuviera descansado y todo eso.
“Pero no fue así. Tuvimos que pelear para meternos, y para hacer lo que teníamos que hacer para entrar, tuvimos que hacerlo básicamente en cada juego de la serie”, señaló.
El núcleo de los Filis —Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Zack Wheeler y Aaron Nola— ha llegado a los playoffs cinco años seguidos y promedió 91 victorias por temporada en ese tramo. Aún no han ganado un campeonato y cada año Filadelfia se ha quedado más lejos de ese objetivo desde que alcanzó la Serie Mundial de 2022.
La temporada siguiente, se despidió en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional, y los dos años posteriores terminaron con derrotas en la serie divisional. Una eliminación en comodines esta temporada representa otro paso en la dirección equivocada.
“Obviamente, nos encantaría ganar una Serie Mundial con estos muchachos. Hemos estado juntos bastante tiempo, tenemos un buen clubhouse y, ya sabes, buenos tipos en este equipo", manifestó Nola. "Sabemos qué clase de personas hay aquí. Sabemos qué clase de peloteros tenemos y de lo que somos capaces. Necesitamos jugar bien en el momento adecuado”.
La racha de cinco años incluyó dos triunfos de serie de playoffs sobre los Bravos. Filadelfia eliminó a Atlanta en 2022 y 2023 pese a que los Bravos ganaron el Este de la Liga Nacional en ambas temporadas. Ese escenario se repitió este año: los Bravos obtuvieron la ventaja de local en esta serie gracias a otro título del Este de la Liga Nacional.
Esta vez, sin embargo, Atlanta consiguió los batazos grandes y el pitcheo oportuno. Ray Kerr, en apenas su décima aparición del año y su primera de postemporada, cumplió a la perfección el papel de abridor. Lanzó 3 1/3 entradas, sin permitir carreras, con una base por bolas y un hit, para preparar el relevo largo de Grant Holmes.
Michael Harris II conectó un jonrón de tres carreras ante Nola en la primera entrada, y los Filis estuvieron a la zaga el resto de la noche.
Estuvieron abajo en su división en abril, pero con el tiempo enderezaron el rumbo. Mattingly asumió el mando cuando Rob Thomson fue despedido el 28 de abril tras un inicio de 9-18.
Los Filis ganaron ocho de sus siguientes nueve juegos y llegaron a .500 el 16 de mayo. Un agosto al rojo vivo los puso en posición de playoffs, pero el boleto de postemporada no se aseguró sino hasta el último juego de la temporada regular.
Mattingly esquivó las preguntas sobre su futuro después del partido.
“No es el momento de hablar de eso. Me siento cómodo con lo que quieran hacer. De nuevo, quiero lo mejor para los Filis. Me encantó estar en Filadelfia este año", indicó. "De hecho, me gusta jugar en ese ambiente. Me gusta el ambiente. Es un ambiente duro, pero es bueno. Otra vez, creo que dejas que la organización evalúe, hable sobre lo que piensa de cara al futuro, lo que debería hacer, y eso determina muchas cosas diferentes”.
_____
Deportes AP: https://apnews.com/hub/deportes

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Bryce Harper Talks Future After Playoff Elimination, Phillies 'Will Look a Lot Different' in 2027
item.dc:creator: Andrew Peters

item.content:encoded:
Bryce Harper Talks Future After Playoff Elimination, Phillies 'Will Look a Lot Different' in 2027
The Philadelphia Phillies' season ended in the American League Wild Card round on Thursday after a 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves.
The Phillies have plenty of questions heading into the offseason, and Bryce Harper expects the team to "look a lot different" in 2027.
"Each year's so different than the year before. I don't really put stock into years before or what happened or anything else," Harper said. "This was a brand new team. Obviously, we had the guys that are part of that core group that we are. I'd imagine this team is going to look a lot different next year with the guys that are leaving this clubhouse. So, we'll see."
Harper is tied to the Phillies through the 2031 season, so he'll remain in Philadelphia for years to come, barring a trade. Stars like Zack Wheeler, Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Aaron Nola are also set to return.
But the Phillies have a handful of notable free agents, such as Alec Bohm, Jose Alvarado, Luis Arreaz, Emundo Sosa and more.
Perhaps the biggest question mark is who will be the Phillies' skipper in 2027.
Philadelphia fired manager Rob Thomson in April after a rough start to the season, and interim manager Don Mattingly helped the Phillies get back on track to reach the postseason, but he has yet to shed the interim tag.
Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported this week that Mattingly was "likely to be replaced" if the Phillies didn't make a deep run in the postseason, so it seems Philadelphia will be on the hunt for a new manager.
Schwarber spoke highly of Mattingly after the season ended on Thursday.
"Even when things got hard, the way that he was able to keep things at even-keel pace for us. I think that was huge," Schwarber said.
The Phillies were interested in Alex Cora after he was fired by the Boston Red Sox, but he turned the offer down. Cora said in April that he's interested in getting back into baseball at some point, but didn't clarify how soon that would be.
Even with an offseason full of changes coming, the Phillies will retain most of their core as they try to get back to the World Series. How different the team will look in the spring remains to be seen.

item.title: [onpattison.com] Figuring out how to fix Trea Turner should be priority No. 1 for Phillies this offseason

item.description: ATLANTA — The question of the cause of the Phillies year-over-year offensive decline had barely been finished being asked before Trea Turner had an answer. “Me,” he said without hesitation. “I mean, it’s pretty simple. When you hit first or second, you get a lot of at-bats, and I kinda get things going. So a lot of that is on me. I think Kyle and Bryce did a good job, I scored a lot of runs, and that’s mostly because those two guys had good years. I think it starts with me and I take a lot of re
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — The question of the cause of the Phillies year-over-year offensive decline had barely been finished being asked before Trea Turner had an answer.
“Me,” he said without hesitation. “I mean, it’s pretty simple. When you hit first or second, you get a lot of at-bats, and I kinda get things going. So a lot of that is on me. I think Kyle and Bryce did a good job, I scored a lot of runs, and that’s mostly because those two guys had good years. I think it starts with me and I take a lot of responsibility for that.”
Just about any way you slice it, it was a disastrous year for Turner. The season came to an end Thursday as the Phillies were eliminated by the Atlanta Braves in the NLWCS.
A year after winning the NL batting title by hitting .304, Turner finished the 2026 season with a lower on-base percentage (.297) than his batting average from the prior campaign. He did homer 19 times, but after posting a .798 OPS across his first three seasons with the Phillies, Turner finished 2026 with a .675 OPS.
Defensively, he had a major bounce back in 2025, posting two defensive runs saved, 16 outs above average and making just eight errors across 1,216 1/3 innings. In 2026, he made 21 errors, while finishing the season with minus-17 defensive runs saved and minus-eight outs above average.
President of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski did once trade Prince Fielder — just two seasons into a nine-year/$214 million contract — to the Texas Rangers for Ian Kinsler. Even though the Tigers had to send $30 million to Texas, it was one of the finest trades of Dombrowski’s career, as he offloaded a bad contract and acquired a tremendous player in the process. Perhaps Dombrowski could facilitate a similar deal this offseason, even if the Phillies don’t get nearly as much back for Turner, who is still owed more than $189 million over the next seven seasons. Of course, Turner would have to sign off on moving, as his deal includes a full no-trade clause.
Assuming Turner is back, the Phillies will have to decide whether they believe he can continue to play shortstop or not. If they believe the answer is no, the Phillies will have to A) decide what position on the field they want to move Turner to and B) sell him on the plan. Even if they can compel him to change positions, they will want him to be bought in on his new position, be it second base, left field or somewhere else.
The bigger issue wherever Turner plays defensively and hits in the lineup might be getting him back on track mentally. He’s a smart guy, one who likes to dig deep into things to try to get out of a slump. While admirable, perhaps that’s to his detriment. Turner will play next season at 34 years old, so he may not quite be at his peak athleticism anymore. But he’s still really capable in that department. The bigger issue this year, particularly in the field, seemed to be his ability to actually make the play when he put himself in position to do so. Figuring out how to help a guy mentally might be harder than teaching him a new position defensively.
Turner has been open this season about his underperformance in 2026. So what will he do this offseason to try to reset?
“That’s a good question,” Turner acknowledged. “I’ve got a lot of work to do. Kinda just go over everything and just figure out as much as I can, find answers, see what I did badly. But I feel like this year is the biggest question mark for me offensively in a long time. I gotta figure that out. I’m definitely gonna have a lot of work to do there, and I’ll do it.”

Sale finished the series against the Phillies as well. The Braves won on Thursday night, 6-2, but it was Sale who pitched the final 1.1 innings for Atlanta to end the game and send them to the NLDS against the Los Angeles Dodgers. item.content:encoded:
Chris Sale got things started for the Atlanta Braves by starting Game 1 against the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round.
Sale finished the series against the Phillies as well.
The Braves won on Thursday night, 6-2, but it was Sale who pitched the final 1.1 innings for Atlanta to end the game and send them to the NLDS against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
As it turns out, Sale is the first pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since 2018. The other one to do it in 2018? It was Chris Sale himself, when he was with the Boston Red Sox.
Chris Sale of the @Braves is the first MLB pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since he himself did so in the 2018 World Series. pic.twitter.com/7esVOkXBlT
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 2, 2026
In 2018, Sale started Game 1 of the World Series against the Dodgers, although he went just four innings and allowed three runs as the Red Sox won 8-4.
Sale then pitched the final inning of Game 5 as the Red Sox won the World Series.
Here was the scene from Thursday night.
Chris Sale sends the @Braves to the NLDS! #CLINCHED
(MLB x @BudweiserUSA) pic.twitter.com/gaa66CiYCy
Exactly one week ago, the @RedSox finished their most dominant season. pic.twitter.com/nqYzeKI0LD
— MLB (@MLB) November 5, 2018
Braves manager Walt Weiss used a total of six pitchers on Thursday night in a win-or-go-home scenario, and Sale threw 21 pitches to keep Atlanta's season alive.
The Braves face the Dodgers on Saturday in Game 1 and Sunday in Game 2, and it will be interesting to see when Sale gets his next start.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees beat the Boston Red Sox by a score of 9-2.
With the victory, they swept the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series.
Bob Nightengale of USA Today wrote: “The New York Yankees sweep the Boston Red Sox out of the Bronx in humiliating fashion. They outscored the Red Sox 18-2 in the wild-card series. They are off to Tampa Bay for a best-of-five AL Division Series beginning Saturday”
Judge Makes Bellinger Statement After Sweep
Cody Bellinger finished the win with two hits, including one home run and four RBIs.
After the game, Aaron Judge was asked about Bellinger when he spoke to YES Network.
Meredith Marakovits: “Last night it was Ben Rice. Tonight it was Cody Bellinger with some big hits. Those two bats in the lineup. Just how valuable are they?”
Judge: “It’s amazing. We saw Ben Rice make a lot of strides last year. I knew coming into this year he’s going to have a great year for us. And then that’s why we signed back Cody Bellinger, man. He’s built for this. He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment. And he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Looking At Bellinger
Bellinger is in the middle of his second season with the Yankees.
He has also spent time with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs over 10 seasons at the MLB level.
As Judge alluded to, Bellinger signed a big deal with the Yankees over the offseason.
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees finished the regular season as the second-place team in the American League East with a 93-68 record in 161 games.
They are looking to win their first World Series title since the 2009 season.
